title: No explicit representation of the generator distribution
description: The adversarial framework does not provide an explicit density p_g(x); only samples can be drawn from the generator. The authors list this as a primary disadvantage relative to previous modeling frameworks.
canonical_description: generator provides no explicit density representation, only samples

verdict.reasoning: The semi-implicit generator (SIG) paper makes genuine but partial progress: it replaces discriminator-based adversarial training with a maximum-likelihood objective by modeling an explicit conditional layer over an implicit latent mixing distribution, trained by minimizing a Monte-Carlo upper bound on the cross-entropy. This gives a density-based training path for an implicit generative model, and it is shown to stabilize GANs when added as a regularizer. However, the paper itself states that the implicit mixing distribution p_φ(θ) cannot be evaluated pointwise and that the marginal P_model(x;φ) is implicit, so no explicit, closed-form density p_g(x) is produced; likelihood evaluation is only approximate (exact only as M→∞), and on complex data the method falls back to the adversarial GAN-SI framework. The second paper is a nonparametric convergence-rate analysis of noise-convolved VAE-type estimators and does not address the generator's missing explicit density — it even acknowledges the noiseless generator density may not exist. Thus the core of the gap — an explicit, evaluable density for the generator — remains open, though the likelihood-based training limitation has been meaningfully advanced.

paper.title: Semi-Implicit Generative Model
paper.abstract: To combine explicit and implicit generative models, we introduce semi-implicit generator (SIG) as a flexible hierarchical model that can be trained in the maximum likelihood framework. Both theoretically and experimentally, we demonstrate that SIG can generate high quality samples especially when dealing with multi-modality. By introducing SIG as an unbiased regularizer to the generative adversarial network (GAN), we show the interplay between maximum likelihood and adversarial learning can stabilize the adversarial training, resist the notorious mode collapsing problem of GANs, and improve the diversity of generated random samples.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes the semi-implicit generator (SIG), a hierarchical model x_i ~ p(x|θ_i) with an explicit conditional p(x|θ) and an implicit mixing distribution p_φ(θ) generated by a neural net transform. Because the conditional layer is explicit and the implicit θ can be MC-sampled, SIG can be trained in a maximum-likelihood framework by minimizing a Monte-Carlo upper bound H_M of the true cross-entropy (which converges to the true objective as M→∞), thereby giving a density-based training objective without a discriminator. The paper also adds SIG as a likelihood regularizer to GANs (GAN-SI), mainly to stabilize training and mitigate mode collapse.
assessments.what_remains_open: SIG does not actually provide an explicit, closed-form density p_g(x) for the generator: the paper explicitly states that p_φ(θ) cannot be evaluated pointwise and that the marginal P_model(x;φ) is implicit. Training is performed on an MC estimate / upper bound of the marginal likelihood (H ≥ H_{M+1} ≥ H_M, exact only in the M→∞ limit), so the model only offers approximate pointwise likelihood evaluation rather than an explicit density representation. Moreover, when scaled to complex data, the paper falls back on the adversarial framework (GAN-SI), which again relies on a discriminator and sample-based training; the main demonstrated benefit there is reduced mode collapse and stabilized optimization, not an explicit generator density. Thus the gap's specific problem — an explicit, evaluable density for the generator — remains unaddressed except in this semi-implicit, MC-estimated form.
evidence_snippets: An implicit generative model, on the other hand, generates its random samples via a stochastic procedure but may not allow a point-wise evaluable PDF, which often makes a direct optimization in [REF:eq:obj] become infeasible.

Here $p(\xv_i\given\thetav_i)$ is required to be explicit but $p_{\phiv}(\thetav_i)$ can be defined by sampling a random variable $\zv_i$ from fixed distribution $p(\zv)$ and setting $\thetav_i = g_{\phiv}(\zv_i)$, where $g_{\phiv}: \cZ \to \cX$ is a deterministic mapping represented by neural network with parameter $\phiv$. paper.title: Minimax optimal density estimation using a shallow generative model with a one-dimensional latent variable
paper.abstract: A deep generative model yields an implicit estimator for the unknown distribution or density function of the observation. This paper investigates some statistical properties of the implicit density estimator pursued by VAE-type methods from a nonparametric density estimation framework. More specifically, we obtain convergence rates of the VAE-type density estimator under the assumption that the underlying true density function belongs to a locally Hölder class. Remarkably, a near minimax optimal rate with respect to the Hellinger metric can be achieved by the simplest network architecture, a shallow generative model with a one-dimensional latent variable.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper analyzes the statistical convergence rate of a VAE-type (likelihood-based) implicit density estimator built from ReLU generative models. Its estimated quantity is the noise-convolved density p_{g,σ}(x) = ∫ φ_σ(x − g(z)) dz, and it proves a near-minimax Hellinger rate n^{-β/(2β+d)} (up to log factors) for a sieve MLE over a shallow network class with a one-dimensional latent variable, with extensions to deep/composite generators. This is a nonparametric density-estimation theory contribution for likelihood-based generative models, not a treatment of the explicit-density limitation of generators.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem — that the adversarial/generator framework yields no explicit density p_g(x) and only samples can be drawn from the generator — is not addressed. The paper studies VAE-type sieve MLE estimators and explicitly acknowledges that the density of g(Z) itself "may not exist"; it obtains a tractable likelihood only by adding Gaussian noise, so the (noiseless) generator distribution still has no explicit density representation. No GAN/adversarial estimator is considered, and no method is proposed to give an explicit p_g for generator outputs or to compute likelihoods of the generator distribution itself; that limitation remains exactly as stated in the gap.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: The main bottlenecks are not data or compute: standard image/likelihood benchmarks exist and flow/EBM-style models train on modest GPU resources. Methodologically, there are mature partial routes (normalizing flows and autoregressive models give exact densities; semi-implicit and energy-based methods give approximate likelihoods), but the core gap — an explicit, pointwise-evaluable density for an arbitrary implicit GAN generator — is fundamentally intractable because p_g(x) requires marginalizing the latent variable, which has no closed form for typical deep generators. Progress is feasible only if the problem is narrowed, e.g., to adversarial training of an invertible/flow generator with exact likelihood; that is a focused and measurable subproblem (evaluable via test NLL and sample quality). As stated, the gap is broad and the exact-density goal for general implicit generators would require a fundamental representation change, so full resolution is unlikely, but scoped progress is realistic.
